title: ‘I Discovered’—Ronaldo's Former Manager Rejects Erik ten Hag Criticism
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Amanda Langell9:00 PM ESTCristiano Ronaldo was always praised for his dedication and drive. / Yasser Bakhsh/Getty ImagesTwo weeks after former Manchester United manager Erik ten Hag ripped into Cristiano Ronaldo’s work ethic, Rudi Garcia—perhaps unknowingly—came to the defense of the five-time Ballon d’Or winner with one small revelation: “He was the first to arrive and the last to leave.”

Ten Hag made headlines when he took aim at Ronaldo in two stunning interviews. He first criticized the forward’s training habits, asserting he “didn’t prepare himself” properly for matches during his second spell at Old Trafford. The Dutchman also claimed Ronaldo told his United teammates to “save their legs” in training.

As if that wasn’t enough, Ten Hag soon twisted the knife even deeper. The 56-year-old said Ronaldo could “no longer bring himself” to “get the most out of every day” or be ”fit” enough to play in the Premier League week in and week out.

The accusations go against everything Ronaldo built his career on: long hours in the gym, extreme diets, extra hours on the pitch. It was always work, work and more work for the Portugal legend, from when he was a teenager at Sporting CP to the twilight of his career in Saudi Arabia, according to former boss Garcia.

There is no love lost between Erik ten Hag (left) and Cristiano Ronaldo. / Matthew Ashton/AMA/Getty ImagesThe Frenchman might have only lasted less than a season in charge at Al Nassr, but he still had the privilege of managing Ronaldo. Garcia was the man in the dugout when the Real Madrid icon made his blockbuster move to the Saudi Pro League in January 2023.

He recounted his experience with Ronaldo to The Athletic, focusing on the superstar’s work ethic without even being asked. “It was so easy because he’s a fantastic player; everyone knows that,”  Garcia said.

“But he’s also a very good man and professional. When you see him with his emotions, you know he’s living for football. I discovered that when I saw him training. He was the first to arrive and the last to leave. He’d celebrate the small competitions we had in training like he’d won the Champions League, with his famous celebration.”

Cristiano Ronaldo won his first Ballon d’Or at Manchester United. / Franck Fife/AFP/Getty ImagesGarcia’s input is aligned with the common perception surrounding Ronaldo’s work ethic. The 41-year-old has been subject to his fair share of criticism over the years, but there’s never been widespread claims of laziness or a lack of discipline before Ten Hag’s tirade.
Former United teammate Ben Foster pulled back the curtain on Ronaldo’s habits back in 2025. “He was absolutely always on it, the first one in and last one to leave training,” he told talkSPORT.
“I’d get there early sometimes and he’d already been there. He’d already had all his massages and he’d be in the gym.”

Former Real Madrid teammate Gareth Bale also revealed how obsessive Ronaldo was during their shared days at the Bernabéu. “Whether in training or matches, all he wanted to do was score,” the Welshman said on the Stick to Football podcast. “He was just so driven.”

Gareth Bale (left) and Cristiano Ronaldo enjoyed incredible success at Real Madrid.  / Gonzalo Arroyo Moreno/Getty ImagesRaphaël Varane, who played with Ronaldo at Real Madrid and United, echoed the sentiments. “He cares about everything, every detail. His motivation for every training session, every game, was huge. He was a machine."

It’s hard to ignore the overwhelming evidence that goes against Ten Hag’s claims, especially when you take a look at Ronaldo’s body of work. The forward has won trophies at every club in his iconic career, including five Champions League titles. He is destined to become the first player to ever score 1,000 goals, and just retired from the international stage with 234 appearances and 146 goals for Portugal, both records in men’s international soccer.

With the amount of money, publicity and success Ronaldo has found off the pitch, it’s his drive and desire to further his legacy that keeps him lacing up his boots week in and week out. He could easily be “saving his legs” in retirement, but he is instead still playing the game he loves at age 41, when he has nothing left to prove.
